lesson.title: What a Business Model Is Made Of
lesson.summary: A business model is the company's plan for turning an idea into a profit: who it sells to, what it offers, how it charges, how it produces and delivers, and how it pays for all this. Knowing its parts lets you see where a firm's revenues, costs and funding needs come from before you look at any numbers.

sections.heading: The recipe behind the profits
sections.body_markdown:
Think of a restaurant. The **menu and the customers** it wants to attract are one half of the story. The **kitchen, suppliers, staff and the money to open the doors** are the other half. A **business model** is the whole recipe: how a company intends to create value for customers and capture part of that value as profit.

It is not a financial statement and it is not a forecast. It is the logic that explains *why* the financial statements should look the way they do. Two firms in the same industry can run very different models, so they can show very different margins, asset needs and risks.

sections.heading: The customer-facing features
sections.body_markdown:
These features answer *who pays us, for what, and how?*

- **Target customers and segments.** A **customer segment** is a group of buyers with similar needs or characteristics (for example students, small businesses, or frequent travellers). A useful segment is easy to identify, fairly uniform inside, and reachable through marketing. Slicing the market into too many tiny segments is a common error.
- **Value proposition and product mix.** What the product does for the customer and which features it includes.
- **Pricing strategy.** How the company charges, for example one price for everyone, different versions, or **group pricing**, where price-sensitive segments such as students get a lower price. Group pricing can add revenue from buyers who would not pay the full price.
- **Market share and channels.** How the firm wins customers and gets the product to them.

sections.heading: The behind-the-scenes features
sections.body_markdown:
These features answer *how do we deliver this and pay for it?*

- **Supply chain.** Who performs which tasks, when, and how. A key choice is what to do in-house and what to **outsource** (hand to an outside firm) or **off-shore** (move to another country).
- **Core competencies and resources.** What the firm is unusually good at, and the people, technology and know-how that support it.
- **Partnerships and alliances.** With whom, when and why the firm cooperates.
- **Funding and resource decisions.** How the firm raises and allocates the money needed to operate and grow.
- **Innovation and technology.** How the firm develops new products or processes and which information systems it runs on.

Together, these choices shape the cost structure and how much capital the business needs.

sections.heading: Why an investor or analyst cares
sections.body_markdown:
A business model is usually summarised for outsiders in a business plan. It is a shortened description of how the firm will function and how investors can make money. It also helps expose weak or overly optimistic assumptions.

For analysis, the central question is whether the model is built on **differentiation** (customers pay more for something distinctive), **low cost** (the firm profits by producing cheaply), or both. Once you know the model, you can ask sensible questions. Where does revenue come from? Which costs rise with volume? How much funding is needed? What could break the plan? A model does not guarantee profit, so it must always be checked against the actual financial results.

worked_example.problem: A start-up sells weekly meal-kit boxes by monthly subscription. It targets busy working professionals and gives a discount to university students. A partner company handles packaging and delivery, and the founders raised money from investors to cover the first two years of losses. Describe the key features of this business model.
steps: Customers and segments: working professionals (the main segment) and students (a price-sensitive segment).
Value proposition: convenient, pre-portioned meals that save shopping and planning time.
Pricing strategy: a monthly subscription, plus group pricing through a student discount to earn revenue from buyers with lower willingness to pay.
Channels: online sign-up and home delivery.
Supply chain: packaging and delivery are outsourced to a partner, while the firm keeps menu design and branding in-house.
Funding: investor capital finances early losses until the customer base is large enough to cover costs.
Summarise: revenue comes from recurring subscriptions, costs depend heavily on food and delivery partners, and success depends on keeping subscribers.
worked_example.answer: The model rests on subscription revenue from two segments (professionals and discounted students), a convenience-based value proposition, outsourced delivery, in-house menu and brand, and investor funding to bridge early losses.

exam_traps: Treating a business model as a financial statement or a profit forecast. It is the plan that explains how value is created and captured, not a set of numbers.
Confusing price with cost. A lower price for students reflects their lower willingness to pay, not a lower cost of serving them.
Assuming more segments are always better. Too many tiny segments make marketing unworkable, and a good segment must be identifiable, fairly uniform and reachable.
Listing only customer-side features and forgetting the supply chain, partnerships, core competencies and funding decisions, which are equally part of the model.
Believing a sound business model guarantees profitability. It describes the intended path to profit, which still has to be verified in the results.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes a company's business model?

options.text: An audited record of the revenues earned and costs incurred in the last year
options.explanation: This describes the income statement. A business model explains the logic that produces such results; it is not a record of them.

options.text: A plan for how the firm creates value for customers and earns profit from it
options.explanation: Correct. A business model covers who the customers are, what is offered, how the firm charges, how it delivers and how it funds itself.

options.text: A legal agreement that sets out the rights of the firm's shareholders
options.explanation: This confuses the business model with corporate governance documents, which deal with ownership rights rather than how the firm makes money.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is a decision about the supply chain element of a business model?

options.text: Hiring an outside contractor to assemble the product instead of building a factory
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing what to do in-house versus outsource or off-shore is a supply chain decision about how and by whom tasks are performed.

options.text: Offering a lower price to students than to commercial customers
options.explanation: This is a pricing decision (group pricing), a customer-facing feature, not a supply chain choice.

options.text: Dividing the market by age group and income level
options.explanation: This is customer segmentation, which concerns who the buyers are, not how goods are produced and delivered.

mcqs.stem: A software firm sells its product for about $1,000 to businesses and for about $100 to students through universities. Which is the best explanation for this approach?

options.text: The student version costs roughly ten times less to produce, so a lower price is needed to cover it
options.explanation: This confuses price with cost. The price gap reflects willingness to pay, and the student version is usually not ten times cheaper to produce.

options.text: Students are a separate customer segment, so charging them less is a form of discounting that always lowers total sales
options.explanation: Reverse reasoning. Group pricing aims to add revenue from buyers who would not pay the full price, so it need not lower total sales.

options.text: Students are a price-sensitive segment, so a lower price captures extra revenue from buyers who would not pay $1,000
options.explanation: Correct. This is group pricing: setting different prices for segments with different willingness to pay.

mcqs.stem: A company wants to define customer segments for its new product. Which approach is most consistent with sound segmentation?

options.text: Choose segments that can be clearly identified, are fairly alike inside, and can be reached through marketing
options.explanation: Correct. These are the three tests of a useful segment: identifiable, relatively homogeneous and reachable.

options.text: Create as many narrow segments as possible so that every customer fits only one
options.explanation: This is oversegmentation. Customers can belong to several segments, and very fine slicing makes targeting impractical.

options.text: Define segments only by the customer's age, since age is the easiest trait to measure
options.explanation: Segments can also be based on income, location, lifestyle, behaviour and so on. Restricting to one basis ignores useful criteria.

mcqs.stem: How does a business plan relate to a business model?

options.text: It replaces the model, because the model exists only in the founders' heads and the plan is the real strategy
options.explanation: The plan does not replace the model. It describes the model in a form that outsiders can read.

options.text: It is an audited projection of the firm's cash flows, which the model then restates in words
options.explanation: Reverse and wrong. A business plan is not an audited document; it is a communication tool built from the model.

options.text: It is a shortened description of the model, used to explain to investors how the business works and how they can earn a return
options.explanation: Correct. The plan is a scaled-down version of the model that is also used to spot weak assumptions and to brief new employees.

mcqs.stem: An analyst compares two airlines. Airline X wins customers with the lowest fares, a single aircraft type and minimal onboard service. Airline Y charges higher fares and offers roomier seats, lounges and premium service. Which pair of business-model features most directly separates the two firms?

options.text: Their legal form and their country of incorporation
options.explanation: Both could share these features. The difference described concerns how each firm creates value and charges for it, not legal form.

options.text: Their value proposition and pricing, supported by different cost structures (low-cost versus differentiation)
options.explanation: Correct. X competes on low cost and low price with tight costs, while Y competes through differentiation and charges more for added value.

options.text: Their ability to forecast the economy more precisely than the other
options.explanation: Nothing in the stem suggests forecasting skill differs. This is a distractor unrelated to the stated differences in offer, price and cost.

mcqs.stem: Why is understanding a company's business model useful when analysing its financial statements?

options.text: It guarantees that the firm's reported profits will meet the plan
options.explanation: A model is an intended path to profit. Results must still be checked, and the plan can fail.

options.text: It removes the need to analyse the firm's reported financial results
options.explanation: The model gives context for the numbers but does not replace the analysis of reported results.

options.text: It explains where revenues, costs and funding needs come from, so the numbers can be interpreted in context
options.explanation: Correct. Knowing the customers, pricing, supply chain and funding choices helps explain the pattern of revenue, cost and capital in the statements.

flashcards.back: The firm's plan for how it creates value for customers and earns profit from that value: who it serves, what it offers, how it charges, how it delivers and how it is funded.

flashcards.front: What three tests make a customer segment useful?
flashcards.back: It is easy to identify, its members are fairly alike, and the firm can reach it with marketing. Avoid oversegmenting.

flashcards.front: What is group pricing, and why do firms use it?
flashcards.back: Charging different prices to different customer groups. It lets the firm earn extra revenue from price-sensitive groups, such as students, who would not pay the full price.

flashcards.front: Name key supply-chain choices inside a business model.
flashcards.back: Who performs each task, when, and how, including whether to keep it in-house, outsource it or off-shore it.

flashcards.front: How does a business plan relate to a business model?
flashcards.back: The plan is a shortened description of the model, used to explain the business to investors and others and to expose weak assumptions.
